title: Agent Distraction
content_excerpt: What is easy for humans to skim past in code, agents see as a call to action. They do not know better, latching on to that which is littered across the files read during the planning and research phase of the coding journey. As agents' agency through tools and skills grows the ability for side-quests scales proportionally. Obsolete specs, long resolved bugs, and lagging documentation no longer rest in long forgotten corners of the codebase, but rather are unintentionally ingested as context indirecting and misdirecting the next wave of coders - the agents. This indirection is not free: in the best case it only costs tokens, steps, and time - in the worst case it distracts and grounds the agent on falsehoods leading to incorrect logic and decisions during implementation. Measuring how often agents fall into these traps across millions of monthly sessions is impossible with manual human review - we need an objective signal derivable from the code itself. Inline TODO(bug/...) comments provide the perfect proxy. TODOs tend to be left behind long after the underlying bug is resolved or abandoned, while the linked bug ticket acts as the canonical record. By cross-referencing every TODO an agent encounters against the TODO's bug status and the user's prompt, we can automatically separate valid work from wasted detours at scale. By leveraging the distributed traces of agent interactions across thousands of engineers and over hundreds of millions of individual agent steps, we quantify the impact of TODO distractions in the codebase and how agents act on them: Controlling for developer, codebase complexity, task type, model tier, number of files read, initial prompt length, and the step where the bug reference appeared, using a multi-way fixed-effects regression with developer-clustered standard errors, we see that unprompted bug detours add substantial overhead (all stat sig p<0.0001). title: llm-gemini 0.37
summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.37

Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.

It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:

Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output
Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Hydrogen   $1.50 $0.075 $7.50

Carbon and Argon are the same price, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.

Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.

I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans. Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:

Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.

Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models:

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.

title: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
story_key: story|ver:4.1|title:llmon an llm native markup language now in granite 4 1 3b and 8b
content_excerpt: LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections. To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages. Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview . We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates. JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans. LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. title: codex 0.168.0
summary:
New Features

  • Browse model providers under Sessions → Model providers and choose the default for new chats. (#59541, #59722)
  • Enable features.tui_workspace to view a side conversation beside the main chat. Drag the divider to resize the panes or press leader z to zoom the focused pane. (#58992, #59527, #59595)
  • Attach recordings when using an audio-capable model. Codex skips confirmed rejected recordings on later turns and uses clip duration to keep more short recordings in context. (#59234, #59268)
  • Enable features.image_generation_animation to generate or edit animated GIFs with optional frame count and timing controls. (#59073)
  • Fullscreen Codex displays image previews and pets in tmux on Ghostty and Kitty with allow-passthrough all. (#59579, #59580)
  • Set tui.notification_method = "osc777" for terminal notifications. Approval notifications show longer command previews and distinguish terminal input from network access requests. (#59256)

Bug Fixes

  • Local TUI history and resume pickers filter newly created threads by the signed-in ChatGPT account. (#58918)
  • Open and resumed chats use their saved model provider after you change the default for new chats. (#59503)
  • The TUI renders replies interrupted by tool calls as a single Markdown message and restores reasoning summaries when replaying a conversation. (#59698, #59700)
  • Steering messages reach running turns when sent during the final transcript save or after switching back to a long-running chat. (#58877, #58998)
  • Fuzzy file search gives filename matches more weight so matching parent directories are less likely to crowd them out. (#59709)
  • Idle local MCP servers on Windows leave filesystem I/O available to the rest of Codex. (#59726)

Documentation

  • The app-server reference covers listing model providers, creating custom gateways, and updating gateway, Bedrock, and GCP settings. (#58845, #58876)

Chores

  • Codex warns when features.multi_agent is explicitly configured and points to agents.enabled for disabling subagent tools. (#59479)
  • Contributors can run Bazel CI jobs locally without BuildBuddy credentials. (#59055)

title: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
story_key: story|title:xybench helping with the problem behind the question
content_excerpt: Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench , a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026. A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem : a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed. Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses. The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal. People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask. We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. title: Building strong safety evaluations
summary: Recommendations for designing, running, and reporting safety evaluations, based on our own experiences.
content_excerpt: Safety evaluations inform some of the most consequential decisions we make about an AI model, including whether it’s ready to deploy, which safeguards ship alongside it, and what our next round of safety training and research should focus on. When we say a model is “safer than its predecessor,” we mean that it scored better on a set of evals someone built. But a safety claim is only as sound as the eval behind it, and good ones are hard to build. A safety eval measures a model’s propensity to cause or contribute to harm, whether its response to a request makes harm more or less likely, and how severe that harm would be, rather than measuring specific capabilities. It can cover different types of harm. For example, a user may actively request harmful outputs (such as seeking instructions on how to harm themselves), or they may request outputs that are intended to be harmless, but that come with high risk of unintended harm (such as seeking information on the appropriate dose of a drug). Essentially, a safety eval asks, “Given a specific input, did the model do the right thing?” Like other types of evals, these can be tricky to get right: researchers have repeatedly found that AI evals are easy to game , don’t always measure what they claim to measure, and aren’t documented well enough to reproduce . The results can change depending on whether the questions are multiple-choice or open-ended , or even based on how answer options are ordered . Psychology faced similar issues a decade ago, when large-scale replication projects found that many published findings didn’t hold up, likely at least in part because many original studies relied on small samples and journals favored statistically significant results. In response, the field instituted reforms such as preregistration (writing down hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting or analyzing data), better measurement, and more rigorous statistics, which made measurements more trustworthy and results easier to replicate. Drawing on those reforms, and from our experience building evals at Anthropic , 1 this post shares recommendations for anyone who builds or relies on AI safety evaluations, using examples from our system cards . It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows. I'm hoping they fix that in the future - it would be great if you could download a single binary and use that as part of a standard test suite in other languages and on other platforms.

title: Which Claude model should you build with? Fable, Opus, Sonnet, or Haiku
summary: Which Claude model to pick, what they cost, and how to use them together.

content_excerpt: The current Claude lineup has four generally available models: Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs. If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code , you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs. The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium . There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work. Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate. Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model. Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page . When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. When you pick a larger model, for example, you are choosing capability over latency. These are the main trade-offs to think through. Generally, bigger models cost more per token and are more capable, but the cost vs capability trade-off isn't universally true at the task level. A higher price per token doesn't always mean a higher cost per task, or a better result. As we showed in Spending your effort , on Anthropic's runs of Terminal-Bench 3.0, the previous Fable, 5.1, at max scored 58.0%, while Opus 5.5 at high scored 58.9% with half the tokens. title: Kitesurf is now open source

content_excerpt: We introduced Kitesurf , our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer. Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network. Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation. Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly: These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices. Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result. All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together. title: The components of agent memory
summary: For Claude to learn from experience, it has to decide what’s worth remembering before it knows what’s next. Here’s how “dreaming” helps it organize memory and correct mistakes.
content_excerpt: Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward , but it must be lived forward . We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents. As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. The hippocampus plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only some experiences are consolidated into long-term knowledge. Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet rest , the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill those experiences and integrate them into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge. Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed sleep-time compute as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called dreaming (Figure 1). We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization. By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), in-context learning (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and compaction (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window). In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can mark a memory as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called replay , helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory.
